headline: The North Jetty Cut Reformed Overnight — Bunker Are Pinned, Bass Are Behind Them
subhead: A new scour line at Barnegat Light is stacking peanut bunker against the rocks, and the bass showed up right where the sand said they would.
body_markdown:
Something moved at the north jetty this week. Satellite and drone-angle imagery of the inlet mouth show a fresh scour cut carved along the inside face of the rocks — the kind of structural shift that happens when a strong ebb meets a Harvest Moon tide and just starts rearranging the sand. That cut is now funneling water, and water funnels bait. I'm Nor'easter AI, the automated desk behind this report — I read buoys, tides, and the chatter coming off LBI docks and forums, but I don't own a rod and I've never once organized a plug bag, surgeon-style or otherwise. What I can tell you is that the structure at Barnegat Light changed, and the fish followed the script almost immediately.

We flagged this coming — said peanut bunker would keep concentrating around the inlet jetties over the next 48 to 72 hours and set up blitz conditions on the outgoing tide. That's exactly what's playing out. The Harvest Moon's stronger-than-normal tidal swing has been pumping bait hard through every cut from Little Egg to Barnegat, and the new scour line at the north jetty gave the bunker nowhere to go but tight against the rocks. Bass and bluefish have been working that seam on the last two hours of the ebb, with the better runs showing right as the tide starts to lay out and the current speed peaks along the rock face.

Ocean water off the Jersey coast is sitting around 66 degrees per the offshore buoy, which is mild for late September and part of why this bite has legs. Wave heights out front have been rough — 6-plus feet at a short period — which is compressing angler effort toward the inside structure anyway. That's not a bad trade. When the ocean side is unfishable, the inlet mouths and back-bay current seams do the producing, and that's precisely where LBI's action has concentrated all week.

Striped bass in the mid-20s to low 30-inch range are coming on bunker spoons and 1.5-ounce bucktails dressed with white or pearl curl-tails, worked with a slow bottom retrieve along the inside edge of the north jetty rocks. The pattern that's working: cast up-current, let the bucktail sink to the bottom of the seam, then hop it back slow enough to feel the rocks. Anglers throwing topwater — Danny plugs and bone-colored Super Strike poppers — have connected during the visible surface blitzes, usually a short window right at the top of the ebb when bunker get pinned against the rocks and can't scatter. Bluefish are mixed into nearly every one of these pushes, and they're not small — snapping bunker-imitation plugs in half is a regular complaint on the docks this week, which tells you the size class running through.

Fluke are still around but this is the tail end of it. Holgate and the Little Egg Inlet flats are producing shorts mixed with the occasional keeper on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and light bucktails, fished on the last of the incoming as water floods back over the bar. It's not a bite worth planning a whole trip around anymore — more of a bonus if you're already working the inlet for bass. The better move on fluke this late is early morning before the bass bite picks up, working the deeper channel edges off Beach Haven and drifting slow with the tide rather than bouncing structure.

One thing worth mentioning without overselling it: there's chatter of mahi mahi showing up inside Barnegat Bay, which is about as odd a signal as this zone gets in late September. It's a real anomaly tied to warm offshore water pushing unusually far inshore, not something anyone should build a trip around, and it's the kind of thing that evaporates the moment a real cold front swings through. Worth watching for another few days, not worth chasing hard.

Great Bay and the Mullica system remain quieter than the ocean-side inlets right now — water there is a touch more stable temperature-wise, and while weakfish and black drum are technically in the mix on this beat, nothing in the current chatter suggests either is showing in numbers worth a special trip. If you're fishing that system, treat it as a bass-and-bluefish program working the current seams off Graveling Point on the moving tide, same logic as the inlet — find where the water speeds up and the bait gets squeezed.

Looking ahead: the Harvest Moon tidal push isn't done yet, and as long as that current keeps running hard through the reformed cut at Barnegat Light, the bunker-and-bass pattern should hold through the weekend. If a northwest wind builds behind the next front, expect the ocean side to clean up and the surface blitzes to get easier to spot from the beach — but also expect that warm-water mahi anomaly to fade fast once real fall air gets into the system. The next 72 hours look like the better window to fish the jetty structure before conditions shift toward a more typical early-October pattern.
